title: Unseen Passages (Discursive and Case-based Factual)
summary: Section A tests how well you read, infer and interpret two unseen passages: a longer discursive or literary passage and a case-based factual passage that often carries a table or chart. This chapter explains the paper pattern, every question type, a step-by-step reading strategy and how to frame answers that earn full marks.

notes.heading: Paper pattern and marks
notes.html:
Section A (Reading Skills) carries 22 marks in the 80-mark theory paper.

QuestionPassage typeLength (approx.)Marks
Q1Discursive / descriptive / literary passage700–750 words12
Q2Case-based factual passage, often with a table, graph or survey data400–450 words10

Each passage carries a mix of objective items (MCQs, fill in the blank, true/false, choosing the right meaning) and very short answer items (answers of 30–40 words). The vocabulary item asks you to find a word from the passage that matches a given meaning.

notes.heading: Types of passages you may meet
notes.html:
• Factual: reports, information about a place, a process, a scientific idea. Focus on facts, figures and cause–effect.
  • Descriptive: paints a person, place or event. Look for the dominant impression and the writer’s attitude.
  • Discursive: argues a point or weighs both sides of an issue. Identify the thesis, supporting reasons and the conclusion.
  • Literary: an extract from a story, memoir or essay. Watch for tone, mood, figurative language and what a character feels.
  • Case-based with data: a short article plus a table or chart. Questions ask you to read values, compare trends and draw inferences that the data supports.

notes.heading: Question types and how to handle each
notes.html:
TypeWhat it testsHow to answer
Literal / factualLocating informationScan for key words from the question; answer in the passage’s facts but your own sentence.
InferentialReading between the linesCombine two clues; begin with ‘This suggests that…’ or ‘The writer implies…’.
Tone / attitudeWriter’s feelingPick an exact adjective (critical, nostalgic, ironic, objective) and justify with a detail.
VocabularyWord meaning in contextFind the word in the given paragraph; check that it fits grammatically in place of the meaning.
Assertion–reasonLogical linkTest the assertion and the reason separately, then ask whether the reason explains the assertion.
Data interpretationReading tables and graphsQuote the exact figure, compare with another figure, and state the trend.
Title / main ideaOverall understandingChoose the option that covers the whole passage, not just one paragraph.

notes.heading: Step-by-step reading strategy
notes.html:
1. Skim (1 minute): read the first and last paragraphs and the first line of each paragraph to grasp the topic and structure.
  2. Read the questions: underline key words so you know what to look for.
  3. Read closely: mark the line or paragraph that answers each question.
  4. Answer in order: questions usually follow the order of the passage.
  5. Check data questions twice: confirm units, years and the row or column you are reading.
  6. Revise: re-read short answers for grammar and completeness.

Time budget: about 20 minutes for Q1 and 15 minutes for Q2.

notes.heading: Writing full-mark short answers
notes.html:
• Answer in a complete sentence that rephrases the question stem.
  • Use your own words; lifting long sentences may lose the expression mark.
  • Stay within 30–40 words for 2-mark answers; one clear point plus one supporting detail is enough.
  • For ‘why’ questions, give the reason; for ‘how’ questions, describe the manner or process.
  • For MCQ-style items write the option letter and the text of the option, e.g. ‘(b) cautious optimism’.

notes.heading: Do’s and don’ts
notes.html:
Do

  • Base every answer only on the passage, not on outside knowledge.
  • Note qualifiers like ‘most’, ‘only’, ‘rarely’ and ‘not’ in options.
  • Use the paragraph number given in vocabulary questions.

Don’t

  • Don’t choose an option just because it repeats words from the passage; distractors often do.
  • Don’t leave any objective item blank; there is no negative marking.
  • Don’t write long paragraphs for a 1-mark item.

notes.heading: Worked example: a short case-based passage
notes.html:
A survey of 1,200 senior-secondary students in four cities asked how they spend the first hour after school. Thirty-eight per cent said they go straight to coaching classes, while 27 per cent spend the hour on their phones. Only 14 per cent play an outdoor sport, a figure that falls to 9 per cent among girls. Counsellors who reviewed the findings warned that the shrinking time for unstructured play may be linked to the rise in stress complaints reported by school clinics. They suggested that schools keep playgrounds open for an hour after the final bell.

Activity in first hourStudents (%)
Coaching classes38
Phone / social media27
Homework at home21
Outdoor sport14

Q. What inference can be drawn from the data about girls?
A. Girls are even less likely than the average student to play outdoors after school, since only 9 per cent of them do so against 14 per cent overall, which suggests that safety or social barriers limit their access to play.

keyTerms.definition: Reading quickly to get the general idea or gist of a passage.
Searching a passage rapidly for a specific fact, figure or key word.
A conclusion reached from clues in the passage when the writer does not state it directly.
The writer’s attitude towards the subject, e.g. sarcastic, sympathetic, objective, alarmed.
A passage that discusses an issue, often presenting arguments for and against before reaching a view.
A factual passage built around a real-life situation, survey or data set, frequently accompanied by a table or chart.
A wrong option in an MCQ designed to look correct, often by repeating passage words out of context.
A question that gives a statement (assertion) and an explanation (reason) and asks whether each is true and whether the reason explains the assertion.

mcqs.q: In CBSE English Core, how many marks does Section A (Reading Skills) carry?
mcqs.explanation: Section A has two passages worth 12 and 10 marks, totalling 22 marks. 18 is Writing and 40 is Literature.

mcqs.q: Read: “The old ferryman had crossed the river ten thousand times, yet each dawn he studied the current as if it were a stranger.” What does the sentence suggest about the ferryman?
options: He was humble and careful despite experience.
He was new to the job.
mcqs.explanation: Studying a familiar current ‘as if it were a stranger’ shows humility and caution. He is experienced (ten thousand crossings), so options about forgetting or being new contradict the text.

mcqs.q: Read: “Cities that plant one tree for every resident report summer street temperatures up to four degrees lower than those that do not.” Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Trees always reduce temperatures by four degrees.
Tree planting can help cool urban streets.
mcqs.explanation: The sentence says up to four degrees, so ‘always’ overstates it. The safe inference is that tree planting can help cool streets; the other options are not supported.

mcqs.q: A question asks for ‘the tone of the writer’ in a passage that mocks officials who inaugurate the same bridge three times. The most suitable answer is:
mcqs.explanation: Mocking repeated, empty ceremonies is satire: humour used to criticise. Reverent and neutral do not fit mockery, and melancholic suggests sadness.

mcqs.q: In a data table, online sales rose from 22% in 2021 to 41% in 2024 while shop sales fell from 78% to 59%. Which statement is correct?
options: Shop sales fell by 41 percentage points.
Online sales nearly doubled their share.
Online sales overtook shop sales by 2024.
mcqs.explanation: 22% to 41% is close to double, so online share nearly doubled. Shop sales fell by 19 points, shop sales are still larger, and the table gives shares, not total sales.

mcqs.q: Assertion (A): Skimming should come before close reading. Reason (R): Skimming gives the overall structure so details are easier to place. Choose the correct option.
options: A is false but R is true.
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A.
A is true but R is false.
Both A and R are true and R explains A.
mcqs.explanation: Both statements are true, and knowing the structure first is the reason skimming comes first, so R correctly explains A.

mcqs.q: Which word from this sentence means ‘lasting a very short time’? “The ephemeral glow of the fireflies faded before the lanterns were even lit.”
mcqs.explanation: Ephemeral means short-lived. ‘Faded’ is a verb describing what happened, not the quality of lasting briefly.

mcqs.q: The best title for a passage is one that:
options: covers the central idea of the whole passage
mcqs.explanation: A title must capture the central idea of the entire passage. A single detail or opening sentence usually covers only part of it.

questions.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

(1) Every monsoon, the lane behind our school turns into a shallow river, and every monsoon the same paper boats appear. Nobody organises them. A child in Class 3 folds one from a torn notebook page, and within an hour a fleet of forty is drifting past the gate, each boat carrying a name scrawled in pencil.

(2) The teachers once tried to ban the boats, worried that children would slip on the wet stones. The ban lasted two days. On the third, the principal herself was seen at the gate, crouching to launch a boat she had folded from a circular about the ban.

(3) What the boats teach is hard to put in a syllabus: that joy can be made from waste, that rules work best when they bend to human nature, and that adults, too, need permission to play.

(a) Why did the teachers ban the boats? (1)
(b) What is ironic about the principal’s action? (2)
(c) Find a word in paragraph 1 that means ‘written hurriedly and carelessly’. (1)
(d) State any two lessons the writer draws from the boats. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) The teachers banned the boats because they feared that children might slip on the wet stones of the flooded lane.

(b) It is ironic because the principal, who had approved the ban, launched a boat herself, and she made it from the very circular that announced the ban. Authority ended up joining the play it had forbidden.

(c) scrawled

(d) The writer learns that joy can be created out of waste material and that rules succeed best when they accept natural human behaviour. (Also acceptable: adults too need permission to play.)

questions.q:
Read the data and answer.

A district library recorded its monthly visitors after opening a free reading corner for teenagers in July: April 2,100; May 2,050; June 1,980; July 2,600; August 3,150; September 3,400.

(a) Describe the trend before and after July. (2)
(b) What can the library reasonably infer? (2)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) Before July, visitor numbers fell slowly from 2,100 to 1,980. After the reading corner opened in July, they rose sharply every month, reaching 3,400 in September, an increase of over 70 per cent from June.

(b) The library can infer that the free teenage reading corner has attracted new visitors, though it should check whether factors such as school holidays also contributed before claiming it as the only cause.

questions.q: Explain, with an example, how you would answer an inferential question in a reading passage. (3)
questions.answerHtml: An inferential question asks for something the writer suggests but does not state. I first locate the relevant lines, then combine the clues with logical reasoning. For example, if a passage says a farmer checks the sky every hour and keeps sacks ready by the door, I infer that he fears rain will ruin his harvest. I begin the answer with ‘This suggests that…’ and support it with the detail from the passage.

questions.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The village of Kothar had lost its pond to a parking lot in 2009. Within five years, the wells ran dry each April. In 2016 a group of retired teachers began digging small recharge pits along the slope above the village. They asked each household for one day of labour a month. By 2022 there were 340 pits, and the wells held water until the monsoon arrived.

(a) What was the immediate effect of losing the pond? (1)
(b) How did the retired teachers involve the community? (2)
(c) What quality of the teachers does the passage highlight? Justify. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) Within five years the village wells began running dry every April.

(b) They asked every household to give one day of labour each month to dig recharge pits, making the project a shared community effort rather than the work of a few.

(c) The passage highlights their perseverance and public spirit. They worked for about six years without official help, creating 340 pits until the wells held water through summer.

questions.q: List four common errors students make in Section A and how to avoid them. (4)
questions.answerHtml:
• Using outside knowledge: answer only from the passage.
  • Choosing options that copy passage words: check whether the meaning, not just the wording, matches.
  • Misreading data: confirm the row, column, year and unit before answering.
  • Over-long answers: keep 2-mark answers to 30–40 words with one point and one detail.
